Neonatal body mass in the Chiriqui brown mouse has been estimated using data from the closely related species Scotinomys teguina, suggesting a birth weight of approximately 2.3 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.3 grams]. This modest initial mass is typical of altricial rodent pups that undergo an extended period of post-natal dependency. Once females reach somatic maturity, they attain a maximum adult body mass of 14 grams [Wwi = 14 grams], which represents a roughly six-fold increase from the neonatal stage. This ultimate wet weight for females is consistent with the relatively small body size characterizing the genus and likely reflects the energetic constraints of a montane insectivorous diet. The developmental trajectory from a 2.3 gram neonate to a 14 gram adult female involves rapid early growth coupled with substantial investment in thermoregulatory capacity.

Under standard metabolic conditions measured at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the basal oxygen consumption of this species has been recorded at 31.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 31.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This maximum basal metabolic rate aligns closely with values predicted for a 14 gram rodent and suggests a relatively high mass-specific metabolic demand, consistent with the species' active foraging lifestyle in cool cloud-forest environments. The elevated BMR may also underpin the short gestation period observed in this lineage, as rapid foetal development requires sustained maternal energy turnover. Comparative data from other small-bodied cricetids indicate that such metabolic rates are near the upper bound for the body mass range, reflecting adaptations to a thermally challenging habitat.

This maximum reproductive rate, documented at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], yields approximately 3 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 3 offspring per year], a notably low reproductive tempo for a rodent of this body size. The extended interbirth interval likely reflects the energetic demands placed on lactating females in a seasonal environment where insect prey availability fluctuates markedly. Such a life-history strategy prioritizes offspring survival over high fecundity, a pattern observed in other small mammals inhabiting unpredictable montane habitats. The total annual recruitment per female is therefore modest, and population growth is correspondingly slow.

The developmental milestones from parturition to nutritional independence proceed rapidly relative to the species' overall lifespan. Gestation time at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] lasts approximately 33 days [tg = approximately 33 days], a standard duration for a rodent of approximately 14 grams [Wwi = approximately 14 grams]. Following birth, the time since birth at weaning is only 7 days [tx = 7 days], recorded at the same body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This extremely abbreviated suckling period is among the shortest documented for any cricetid rodent and suggests that neonates are capable of transitioning to solid food remarkably early. Such rapid weaning may be an adaptation to reduce the mother's energetic burden during the breeding season, allowing her to regain body condition quickly. The post-weaning juvenile stage then extends for a prolonged interval before the onset of reproductive maturity.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs relatively late in life when considered in the context of the abbreviated weaning period. Puberty is attained at 78 days since birth [tp = 78 days since birth] when animals are maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The maximum lifespan, extrapolated from data on the closely related hispid cotton rat Sigmodon hispidus, is estimated at approximately 5.2 years [am = approximately 5.2 years] under the same thermal regime of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This extended longevity for a rodent of only 14 grams underscores a slow-paced life history that balances low reproductive output with high adult survival. The seven-week delay between weaning and puberty likely allows juveniles to accumulate sufficient body reserves and experience a full seasonal cycle before initiating reproduction, a strategy that buffers against reproductive failure in an unpredictable environment.
